yields.label: Population
yields.definition: Residents counted by the 2024 general census of population and housing (RGPH 2024), all 12 regions.

yields.label: Food
yields.definition: Value added of the primary sector (agriculture, forestry and fishing) in 2024, current dirhams, from the regional accounts.
yields.source: HCP, Note d'information sur les comptes régionaux de l'année 2024 (juillet 2026), annexe 1

yields.label: Production
yields.definition: Value added of the secondary sector (industry, mining, energy, water and construction) in 2024, current dirhams.
yields.source: HCP, Note d'information sur les comptes régionaux de l'année 2024 (juillet 2026), annexe 1

yields.label: Gold (GDP)
yields.definition: Gross domestic product in 2024, current dirhams, by region where the output is produced. The national total includes a small amount HCP does not assign to any region.
yields.source: HCP, Note d'information sur les comptes régionaux de l'année 2024 (juillet 2026), annexe 1

yields.label: Science (schooling)
yields.definition: Average years of schooling of residents aged 25 and over, from the 2024 census. HCP publishes no count of research or technical workers by region, so schooling stands in for science.
yields.source: HCP, RGPH 2024 — 'Caractéristiques démographiques et socioéconomiques de la population, note sur les principaux résultats' (décembre 2024), figure 8

yields.label: Culture (tourist nights)
yields.definition: Nights spent in tourist accommodation establishments in 2024, by region, as counted by the Ministry of Tourism.
yields.source: Ministère du Tourisme, de l'Artisanat et de l'Economie Sociale et Solidaire, Chiffres clés — 'Evolution par région des nuitées réalisées dans les établissements d'hébergement touristique' (xlsx)

yields.label: Unemployment rate
yields.definition: Unemployed as a share of the labour force aged 15 and over, national employment survey 2024. HCP publishes the three southern regions as one group. The Unemployment lens uses the 2024 census rate instead, which exists for all 12 regions and runs higher.
yields.source: HCP, Enquête nationale sur l'emploi — note 'Situation du marché du travail en 2024' (tableau 2) et rapport 'Activité, emploi et chômage, résultats annuels 2024' (tableaux 7.1 et 8.1)

lenses.label: Population
lenses.note: Residents per km², by province or prefecture. Colour scale is logarithmic.
lenses.source: HCP, censuses of 2014 and 2024 (RGPH 2024); areas from citypopulation.de

lenses.label: Growth
lenses.note: Average yearly population change between the 2014 and 2024 censuses, by province. Some changes reflect boundary changes. The scale stops at the 5th and 95th percentiles.

lenses.label: GDP per head
lenses.note: Regional GDP divided by population, 2024, current dirhams, as published by HCP.
lenses.source: HCP, Note d'information sur les comptes régionaux de l'année 2024 (juillet 2026), annexe 1

lenses.label: Household spending
lenses.note: Household final consumption spending per resident, 2024, current dirhams.
lenses.source: HCP, Note d'information sur les comptes régionaux de l'année 2024 (juillet 2026), annexe 1

lenses.label: Regional GDP
lenses.note: Gross domestic product of the region, 2024, current dirhams. Colour scale is logarithmic.
lenses.source: HCP, Note d'information sur les comptes régionaux de l'année 2024 (juillet 2026), annexe 1

lenses.label: Farming share
lenses.note: Agriculture, forestry and fishing as a share of the region's GDP, 2024.
lenses.source: HCP, Note d'information sur les comptes régionaux de l'année 2024 (juillet 2026), annexe 1

lenses.label: Industry share
lenses.note: Industry, mining, energy, water and construction as a share of the region's GDP, 2024.
lenses.source: HCP, Note d'information sur les comptes régionaux de l'année 2024 (juillet 2026), annexe 1

lenses.label: Services share
lenses.note: Services as a share of the region's GDP, 2024.
lenses.source: HCP, Note d'information sur les comptes régionaux de l'année 2024 (juillet 2026), annexe 1

lenses.label: Tourist nights
lenses.note: Nights spent in tourist accommodation establishments in 2024. Colour scale is logarithmic.
lenses.source: Ministère du Tourisme, de l'Artisanat et de l'Economie Sociale et Solidaire, Chiffres clés — 'Evolution par région des nuitées réalisées dans les établissements d'hébergement touristique' (xlsx)

lenses.label: Unemployment
lenses.note: Unemployment rate from the 2024 census, for all 12 regions. It runs higher than the employment-survey rate (13.3% nationally), which counts joblessness more strictly. Some regional values were read from a chart in the HCP note and are not repeated in its text.
lenses.source: HCP, RGPH 2024 — 'Caractéristiques démographiques et socioéconomiques de la population, note sur les principaux résultats' (décembre 2024), figure 14

lenses.label: Poverty
lenses.note: Share of residents in multidimensional poverty (health, education and living conditions), 2024.
lenses.source: HCP, Base de données de la cartographie de la pauvreté multidimensionnelle (RGPH 2024 & 2014), mai 2025

lenses.label: Monetary poverty
lenses.note: Share of residents below the national monetary poverty line, 2022 living-standards survey.
lenses.source: HCP, 'Evolution du niveau de vie de la population à la lumière des résultats de l'Enquête Nationale sur le Niveau de Vie des Ménages de 2022' (juin 2024), graphique 6

lenses.label: Urban share
lenses.note: Share of residents living in urban areas, 2024 census.
lenses.source: HCP, Population légale du Royaume d'après le RGPH 2024 (note de novembre 2024, tableaux 2 et 3)

lenses.label: Schooling
lenses.note: Average years of schooling of residents aged 25 and over, 2024 census. Some regional values were read from a chart in the HCP note and are not repeated in its text.
lenses.source: HCP, RGPH 2024 — 'Caractéristiques démographiques et socioéconomiques de la population, note sur les principaux résultats' (décembre 2024), figure 8

lenses.label: Secondary or more
lenses.note: Share of residents aged 25 and over who reached at least lower-secondary school, 2024 census. Some regional values were read from a chart in the HCP note and are not repeated in its text.
lenses.source: HCP, RGPH 2024 — 'Caractéristiques démographiques et socioéconomiques de la population, note sur les principaux résultats' (décembre 2024), figure 9

lenses.label: Illiteracy
lenses.note: Share of residents aged 10 and over who cannot read and write, 2024 census. Some regional values were read from a chart in the HCP note and are not repeated in its text.
lenses.source: HCP, RGPH 2024 — 'Caractéristiques démographiques et socioéconomiques de la population, note sur les principaux résultats' (décembre 2024), figure 10

resources.name: Khouribga phosphate basin (Ouled Abdoun)
resources.note: OCP's main mining basin and Morocco's largest phosphate deposit; it supplied about 18 of the 28.4 Mt of phosphate rock Morocco produced in 2012.

resources.name: Sidi Chennane phosphate mine
resources.note: OCP open-pit phosphate mine in the Khouribga (Ouled Abdoun) basin, opened in October 1994.

resources.name: Benguerir phosphate mine (Gantour basin)
resources.note: OCP open-pit phosphate mine in the Gantour basin, about 70 km north of Marrakech, in production since 1979-80; ore goes to the Safi and Jorf Lasfar chemical plants.

resources.name: Bou Craa phosphate mine
resources.note: Phosboucraa (OCP subsidiary) mine in Laayoune-Sakia El Hamra on a deposit of over 1.7 billion tonnes, mined since 1972; about 3 Mt a year, roughly 10% of national output.

resources.name: Imiter silver mine
resources.note: Managem's historic silver mine east of Boumalne-Dades, operating since 1969; produced 127 t of silver in 2025.

resources.name: Zgounder silver mine
resources.note: Aya Gold & Silver's mine near Jebel Siroua; with 4.82 million ounces (about 150 t) in 2025 it overtook Imiter as Morocco's largest silver mine.

resources.name: Bou Azzer cobalt mine
resources.note: Managem's Bou Azzer is Morocco's only active cobalt mine; 507 t of cobalt cathodes in 2025 (down 61% on 2024), with a cobalt-sulphate unit due to lift 2026 output.

resources.name: Tizert copper mine
resources.note: Managem mine in Taroudant province that entered production in 2025 and became Morocco's largest copper mine; 33,824 t of concentrate plus 24 t of silver in its ramp-up year.

resources.name: Bleida copper mine
resources.note: Managem copper operation in Zagora province; the Bleida site produced 31,514 t of copper concentrate in 2025 (Mindat lists the original Bleida pit, used here for coordinates, as mined out).

resources.name: Akka mine
resources.note: Managem's Akka mining site produced 34,294 t of copper concentrate in 2025; point is Akka town, not the pit itself.

resources.name: Hajar polymetallic mine (Guemassa)
resources.note: Massive-sulphide (polymetallic) deposit in the Guemassa massif about 35 km south-west of Marrakech; current operating status not verified.

resources.name: Tighza mine (Jbel Aouam)
resources.note: Lead-zinc-silver vein deposit (with tungsten-molybdenum) at Jbel Aouam near M'rirt in central Morocco; current operating status not verified.

resources.name: El Hammam fluorite mine
resources.note: Fluorite mine about 43 km south-west of Meknes, described by Mindat as the only fluorite mine in Morocco; current operating status not verified.

resources.name: Imini manganese mine
resources.note: SACEM's Imini mine near Ouarzazate is Morocco's main manganese mine, producing about 90,000 t a year, mostly for the chemical industry.

resources.name: Mibladen mining district
resources.note: Former lead mining district about 25 km north of Midelt, world-famous for vanadinite crystals; industrial mining stopped in 1975 and only artisanal collecting continues.

resources.name: Jerada coal basin
resources.note: Morocco's former coal basin in the Oriental region; the state mines were shut in the 1990s (French Wikipedia gives 1990) and informal digging in abandoned shafts continues.

resources.name: Noor Ouarzazate I (CSP)
resources.note: First phase of the MASEN/ACWA Power Noor Ouarzazate complex: a parabolic-trough concentrated solar plant with storage.

resources.name: Noor Ouarzazate II (CSP)
resources.note: Second parabolic-trough CSP plant of the Noor Ouarzazate complex (MASEN/ACWA Power).

resources.name: Noor Ouarzazate III (CSP tower)
resources.note: Solar-tower CSP plant of the Noor Ouarzazate complex (MASEN/ACWA Power).

resources.name: Noor Ouarzazate IV (PV)
resources.note: Photovoltaic phase of the Noor Ouarzazate complex (MASEN/ACWA Power); the four phases total about 580 MW.

resources.name: Noor Midelt I
resources.note: MASEN hybrid PV + CSP project near Midelt (EDF Renewables/Masdar/Green of Africa consortium); Global Energy Monitor still listed it as pre-construction when checked in Nov 2026; coordinates approximate.

resources.name: Noor Laayoune (PV)
resources.note: MASEN/ACWA Power photovoltaic plant at Dcheira near Laayoune.

resources.name: Noor Boujdour (PV)
resources.note: MASEN/ACWA Power photovoltaic plant at Boujdour.

resources.name: Noor Tafilalt Erfoud (PV)
resources.note: ONEE photovoltaic plant, one of three 40 MWp Noor Tafilalt sites.

resources.name: Noor Tafilalt Zagora (PV)
resources.note: ONEE photovoltaic plant, one of three 40 MWp Noor Tafilalt sites.

resources.name: Noor Tafilalt Missour (PV)
resources.note: ONEE photovoltaic plant, one of three 40 MWp Noor Tafilalt sites.

resources.name: Ain Beni Mathar ISCC plant
resources.note: ONEE integrated solar combined-cycle plant: a gas-fired combined cycle of about 470 MW (Wikipedia list) including a 20 MW parabolic-trough solar field (Global Energy Monitor).

resources.name: Tahaddart combined-cycle plant
resources.note: Gas-fired combined-cycle plant south of Tangier (ONEE with Endesa).

resources.name: Jorf Lasfar power station
resources.note: TAQA Morocco's six-unit coal plant, the country's largest power station; units commissioned 1994-2001 with units 5-6 added in 2014.

resources.name: Safi power station
resources.note: Two 693 MW ultra-supercritical coal units owned by Safi Energy Company (Nareva, ENGIE, Mitsui).

resources.name: Mohammedia power station
resources.note: ONEE thermal plant with two 150 MW coal units and two 150 MW oil-fired units.

resources.name: Jerada power station
resources.note: ONEE coal plant; the 350 MW unit 4 dates from 2017, while the three 55 MW units from 1971-72 are listed as retired in 2024.

resources.name: Tarfaya wind farm
resources.note: Tarec (ENGIE/Nareva) wind farm of 131 turbines about 20 km from Tarfaya, one of Africa's largest; point is Tarfaya town because published site coordinates were inconsistent.

resources.name: Akhfennir wind farm
resources.note: Nareva (Energie Eolienne du Maroc) wind farm about 15 km from Akhfennir, built in two phases (102 MW in 2014, 100 MW in 2016).

resources.name: Aftissat wind farm
resources.note: Nareva (Energie Eolienne du Maroc) wind farm south of Boujdour: 202 MW commissioned in 2018 and a 200 MW second phase in 2023.

resources.name: Boujdour wind farm
resources.note: 300 MW wind farm of the ONEE integrated wind programme (Nareva/Enel Green Power), listed as operating since 2023; point is Boujdour town, site coordinates not verified.

resources.name: Midelt wind farm
resources.note: ONEE integrated wind programme site (Nareva/Enel Green Power/Siemens Gamesa consortium) near Midelt.

resources.name: Taza wind farm
resources.note: ONEE/EDF Renewables wind farm; the 87 MW first phase runs since 2022, a 63 MW second phase is still planned.

resources.name: Jbel Khalladi wind farm
resources.note: ACWA Power wind farm about 30 km from Tangier; Wikipedia (citing TelQuel) dates its start to 2018, Global Energy Monitor lists 2021.

resources.name: Tanger I wind farm (Dhar Saadane)
resources.note: ONEE wind farm at Dhar Saadane/Bni Majmel south-east of Tangier, commissioned in two phases (107 MW in 2009, 33 MW in 2011).

resources.name: Amogdoul wind farm (Cap Sim)
resources.note: ONEE wind farm at Cap Sim just south of Essaouira.

resources.name: Haouma wind farm
resources.note: Wind farm of about 51 MW near Ksar Sghir on the Strait of Gibraltar, commissioned in 2014.

resources.name: Foum El Oued wind farm
resources.note: Nareva (Energie Eolienne du Maroc) wind farm at El Marsa near Laayoune.

resources.name: Afourer pumped-storage station (STEP)
resources.note: ONEE pumped-storage scheme in the hills above Afourer (Azilal), built 2001-2004.

resources.name: Abdelmoumen pumped-storage station (STEP)
resources.note: ONEE 2 x 175 MW pumped-storage plant on the Issen river beside the Abdelmoumen reservoir, listed as operating since 2024.

resources.name: Allal al Fassi hydroelectric plant
resources.note: ONEE 3 x 80 MW hydro plant on the Sebou river (Sefrou province).

resources.name: Al Wahda hydroelectric plant
resources.note: ONEE 3 x 80 MW power station at the foot of Al Wahda dam, Morocco's largest reservoir.

resources.name: Bin el Ouidane hydroelectric plant
resources.note: ONEE power station at Bin el Ouidane dam on the El Abid river (Azilal).

resources.name: Al Wahda dam
resources.note: Morocco's largest reservoir, on the Ouergha river north of Fez, built for power, irrigation and water transfer; it feeds a 240 MW hydro plant.

resources.name: Al Massira dam
resources.note: Second-largest reservoir in Morocco, on the Oum Er-Rbia river; supplies drinking water and irrigation and drives a 128 MW hydro plant.

resources.name: Bin el Ouidane dam
resources.note: 133 m high dam on the El Abid river in the Atlas (Azilal province), built for hydropower and irrigation.

resources.name: Idriss I dam
resources.note: Large reservoir on the Inaouen river north-east of Fez, used for irrigation and hydropower.

resources.name: Sidi Mohammed Ben Abdellah dam
resources.note: Drinking- and industrial-water reservoir near Rabat, also used for flood protection; built in 1974 and raised in 2007. Wikidata carries two coordinate values, the one nearer Rabat is used.

resources.name: Oued El Makhazine dam
resources.note: Reservoir on the Loukkos river used for irrigation, water supply and a 36 MW hydro plant.

resources.name: Ahmed El Hansali dam
resources.note: Dam on the upper Oum Er-Rbia river near El Ksiba, with a 92 MW hydro plant.

resources.name: Mansour Eddahbi dam
resources.note: Reservoir just east of Ouarzazate, built in 1972 for irrigation and hydropower.

resources.name: Mohammed V dam
resources.note: Main reservoir on the Moulouya river in eastern Morocco, used for irrigation, drinking water and power.

resources.name: Hassan Addakhil dam
resources.note: Dam at Errachidia built in 1971 for irrigation and flood control.

resources.name: Youssef Ibn Tachfin dam
resources.note: Reservoir on the Massa river in Tiznit province, for irrigation and water supply.

resources.name: El Kansera dam
resources.note: One of Morocco's oldest large dams, on the Beht river (built 1935, raised 1969), for power, irrigation and water supply.

resources.name: Hassan I dam
resources.note: 145 m high dam on the Lakhdar river near Demnate, for irrigation, power and water supply.

resources.name: Abdelmoumen dam
resources.note: Reservoir on the Issen river north-east of Agadir for irrigation, water supply and power; site of the 350 MW Abdelmoumen pumped-storage plant.

resources.name: Tanger Med port
resources.note: Africa's and the Mediterranean's largest container port, on the Strait of Gibraltar; 11.1 million TEU and about 161 Mt of cargo handled in 2025 (Tanger Med Port Authority).

resources.name: Jorf Lasfar port
resources.note: Largest ANP port by tonnage: deep-water bulk port south of El Jadida serving the OCP phosphate-fertiliser complex and the coal power station. Traffic figure from ANP's 2025 port report.

resources.name: Port of Casablanca
resources.note: Second-busiest ANP port, handling about 31% of ANP traffic. Traffic figure from ANP's 2025 port report.

resources.name: Port of Safi
resources.note: Safi city port (ANP 'Safi Ville'). Traffic figure from ANP's 2025 port report.

resources.name: Safi Atlantique (new port of Safi)
resources.note: New deep-water port south of Safi, next to the Safi coal power station. Traffic figure from ANP's 2025 port report.

resources.name: Port of Agadir
resources.note: Commercial port of Agadir and the Souss. Traffic figure from ANP's 2025 port report.

resources.name: Port of Mohammedia
resources.note: Port of Mohammedia, the city that hosts the idle SAMIR refinery. Traffic figure from ANP's 2025 port report.

resources.name: Port of Nador (Beni Ansar)
resources.note: Mediterranean port of Nador at Beni Ansar. Traffic figure from ANP's 2025 port report.

resources.name: Port of Laayoune
resources.note: Port at El Marsa serving Laayoune. Traffic figure from ANP's 2025 port report.

resources.name: Port of Dakhla
resources.note: Existing port of Dakhla (the new deep-water Dakhla Atlantique port is being built about 70 km to the north). Point is Dakhla town. Traffic figure from ANP's 2025 port report.

resources.name: Port of Tan-Tan
resources.note: Small Atlantic port at El Ouatia (Tan-Tan Plage), mainly a fishing harbour with marginal commercial traffic. Traffic figure from ANP's 2025 port report.

resources.name: Nador West Med
resources.note: New deep-water transshipment and energy port in Betoya bay west of Nador; first terminal was due to enter service in late 2026 (press reports through Oct-Nov 2026 conflict on whether it has opened). Wikipedia versions give coordinates a few km apart.

resources.name: Port of Kenitra
resources.note: River port (Port fluvial de Kenitra), listed among Morocco's commercial ports; no recent traffic figure found.

resources.name: Port of Al Hoceima
resources.note: Mediterranean fishing, ferry and marina port of the central Rif; no recent traffic figure found.

resources.name: Laayoune fishing port (El Marsa)
resources.note: ONP recorded 209,954 t of coastal and artisanal landings here in 2025 (up 17%), close to a fifth of the national total of about 1.13 Mt.

resources.name: Dakhla fishing port
resources.note: ONP recorded 57,320 t landed in the first seven months of 2025 (down 21%), with a much steeper fall reported in 2026. Point is Dakhla town.

resources.name: Tan-Tan fishing port
resources.note: Sardine port at El Ouatia; ONP counted 56,355 t in 2024 and reported a 65% rise in 2025, driven by small pelagics.

resources.name: Agadir fishing port
resources.note: ONP coastal and artisanal landings were 36,939 t to end-November 2025, down about 11% on a year earlier.

resources.name: Safi fishing port
resources.note: ONP landings were 43,172 t in the first nine months of 2025, mostly small pelagic fish.

resources.name: Essaouira fishing port
resources.note: Small historic sardine port; ONP landings fell to 16,988 t in 2025 from 25,009 t in 2024.

resources.name: Larache fishing port
resources.note: Fishing port of Larache on the north Atlantic coast; no annual tonnage found (ONP reported a 2% dip to end-November 2025).

resources.name: Boujdour fishing port
resources.note: Southern fishing port tracked by ONP; no annual tonnage found. Point is Boujdour town.

resources.name: Sidi Ifni fishing port
resources.note: Small Atlantic harbour; fishing is the economic base of Sidi Ifni.

resources.name: Casablanca Mohammed V International Airport (CMN)
resources.note: Morocco's busiest airport, at Nouaceur south of Casablanca.

resources.name: Marrakesh Menara Airport (RAK)
resources.note: Second-busiest airport in Morocco (figure rounded).

resources.name: Agadir Al Massira Airport (AGA)
resources.note: Third-busiest airport in Morocco; ONDA counted 3,495,277 passengers in 2025, up 11%.

resources.name: Tangier Ibn Battouta Airport (TNG)
resources.note: Fourth-busiest airport in Morocco (2023 figure, rounded; 2025 traffic was reported up 17%).

resources.name: Fes Saiss Airport (FEZ)
resources.note: Airport of Fez, fifth-busiest in Morocco (2023 figure, rounded).

resources.name: Rabat-Sale Airport (RBA)
resources.note: Airport of the capital; traffic rose about 26% in 2025.

resources.name: Nador Al Aroui Airport (NDR)
resources.note: Airport of Nador, seventh-busiest in Morocco (2023 figure).

resources.name: Oujda Angads Airport (OUD)
resources.note: Airport of Oujda, eighth-busiest in Morocco (2023 figure).

resources.name: Tetouan Sania Ramel Airport (TTU)
resources.note: Small airport serving Tetouan (2023 figure).

resources.name: Laayoune Hassan I Airport (EUN)
resources.note: Airport of Laayoune (2023 figure).

resources.name: Dakhla Airport (VIL)
resources.note: Airport of Dakhla (2023 figure).

resources.name: Essaouira Mogador Airport (ESU)
resources.note: Small airport serving Essaouira (2023 figure).

resources.name: Ouarzazate Airport (OZZ)
resources.note: Airport of Ouarzazate (2023 figure).

resources.name: Errachidia Moulay Ali Cherif Airport (ERH)
resources.note: Regional airport for Errachidia and the Tafilalet; no recent passenger figure found.

resources.name: Al Hoceima Cherif Al Idrissi Airport (AHU)
resources.note: Regional airport of the central Rif coast; no recent passenger figure found.

resources.name: Medina of Fez
resources.note: UNESCO World Heritage Site (cultural), inscribed 1981. Fez was founded in the 9th century and peaked as the Marinid capital; its medina is one of the most extensive and best-preserved old towns in the Muslim world.

resources.name: Medina of Marrakesh
resources.note: UNESCO World Heritage Site (cultural), inscribed 1985. Founded in the 1070s as the Almoravid capital; monuments include the Koutoubia Mosque and Jemaa el-Fnaa square.

resources.name: Ksar of Ait-Ben-Haddou
resources.note: UNESCO World Heritage Site (cultural), inscribed 1987. Fortified earthen village (ksar) on a former trans-Saharan trade route.

resources.name: Medina of Essaouira (formerly Mogador)
resources.note: UNESCO World Heritage Site (cultural), inscribed 2001. Fortified port town founded in the second half of the 18th century and laid out on Vauban's military-engineering principles.

resources.name: Historic City of Meknes
resources.note: UNESCO World Heritage Site (cultural), inscribed 1996. Founded by the Almoravids in the 11th century and made the capital of Sultan Moulay Ismail in the 17th.

resources.name: Medina of Tétouan (formerly known as Titawin)
resources.note: UNESCO World Heritage Site (cultural), inscribed 1997. Link between Morocco and Andalusia from the 8th century, rebuilt by refugees after the Reconquista, with strong Andalusian influence.

resources.name: Portuguese City of Mazagan (El Jadida)
resources.note: UNESCO World Heritage Site (cultural), inscribed 2004. Fortified colony built by the Portuguese in the early 16th century and held until 1769.

resources.name: Archaeological Site of Volubilis
resources.note: UNESCO World Heritage Site (cultural), inscribed 1997. Founded in the 3rd century BCE as a capital of Mauretania, later a Roman outpost and briefly the Idrisid capital.

resources.name: Rabat, Modern Capital and Historic City: a Shared Heritage
resources.note: UNESCO World Heritage Site (cultural), inscribed 2012. The capital rebuilt under the French protectorate from 1912, integrated with older quarters such as the 12th-century kasbah.

resources.name: Saffron - Taliouine
resources.note: Taliouine is famous for its saffron and is one of the main exporters of the spice worldwide.

resources.name: Roses - Kalaat M'Gouna
resources.note: Kalaat M'Gouna is best known for its Rose Festival, held in the town every May.

resources.name: Dates - Erfoud (Tafilalet)
resources.note: Oasis town of the Tafilalet and host of Morocco's international date fair; the Draa-Tafilalet region grows roughly three-quarters of the national date crop (103,000 t forecast for 2024-25).

resources.name: Citrus - Berkane
resources.note: Berkane is a major centre of the citrus industry in northern Morocco.

resources.name: Argan - Souss (Arganeraie Biosphere Reserve)
resources.note: The Souss is the heartland of the endemic argan tree; the Arganeraie was recognised as a UNESCO biosphere reserve in December 1998, covering about 2.57 million ha from Essaouira to Sidi Ifni.

resources.name: Apples - Midelt
resources.note: The Midelt region is best known for its apples (also walnuts, apricots and plums).

resources.name: Cedar forest - Azrou
resources.note: Azrou (1,250 m) is surrounded by mountains covered with holm oak and cedar; the nearby Ifrane National Park is largely Atlas-cedar forest.

resources.name: Almonds - Tafraout
resources.note: Anti-Atlas town surrounded by almond and olive groves, with argan and fig trees.

resources.name: Olives - Kalaat Sraghna
resources.note: The town's economy rests on agriculture, with olive growing predominant.

resources.name: Sugar beet - Sidi Bennour (Doukkala)
resources.note: Sidi Bennour, in the Doukkala plain (wheat, sugar beet, cattle), has Morocco's biggest sugar factory.

resources.name: Cherries - Sefrou
resources.note: Sefrou is known for its annual cherry festival.

resources.name: Lentils - Khemisset
resources.note: The Khemisset region is Morocco's lentil country: about 10,000 ha cultivated and some 100,000 quintals a year.

resources.name: Cereals - Settat (Chaouia)
resources.note: Settat is a main town of the Chaouia, a plain historically famous for its wheat and barley.

resources.name: Red fruits - Larache (Loukkos)
resources.note: The Loukkos perimeter around Larache is Morocco's main strawberry, raspberry and blueberry basin: about 4,000 ha and 130,000 t in 2015-16, some 80% of national output.

resources.name: Tomatoes and early vegetables - Biougra (Chtouka Ait Baha)
resources.note: Chtouka Ait Baha province (capital Biougra) concentrates the tomato farms of Souss-Massa, the region behind the great majority of Morocco's tomato and early-vegetable exports.

resources.name: Cork oak - Maamora forest (Kenitra)
resources.note: The Maamora, spreading across Kenitra, Sidi Slimane and Sidi Kacem provinces, is described as the world's largest continuous cork-oak forest (about 132,000 ha, of which some 70,000 ha cork oak); point is Kenitra town.

resources.name: Wine and olives - Meknes
resources.note: The Meknes-El Hajeb area concentrates most of Morocco's wine production (over 60-75% according to press surveys) and is a leading olive-growing area.

resources.name: Al Boraq high-speed line - Tanger-Ville terminal
resources.note: Northern terminus of Al Boraq, Africa's first high-speed rail service (Tangier-Casablanca), opened on 15 November 2018 by ONCF.

resources.name: Al Boraq high-speed line - Casa-Voyageurs terminal
resources.note: Southern terminus of Al Boraq; trains run on a dedicated high-speed line from Tangier to Kenitra, then on the upgraded main line via Rabat to Casablanca.

resources.name: Renault Tanger Mediterranee plant
resources.note: Renault Group's car plant at Malloussa near Tangier (no production figure verified).

resources.name: Stellantis Kenitra plant
resources.note: Stellantis car plant in the industrial zone at Ameur Seflia east of Kenitra (location from OpenStreetMap; no production figure verified).

resources.name: OCP Jorf Lasfar phosphate complex
resources.note: OCP's phosphoric-acid and fertiliser platform at Jorf Lasfar, fed with phosphate pulp from Khouribga by slurry pipeline since 2014.

resources.name: Khouribga-Jorf Lasfar slurry pipeline (Khouribga head)
resources.note: OCP's 187 km slurry pipeline carrying phosphate pulp from the Khouribga mines to Jorf Lasfar, inaugurated on 2 October 2014; point is Khouribga town.

resources.name: SAMIR refinery (Mohammedia)
resources.note: Morocco's only oil refinery, idle since August 2015 and in court-ordered liquidation since 2016; no restart agreed as of spring 2026. Point is the 'La Samir' stop beside the site.

resources.name: Chtouka (Douira) seawater desalination plant
resources.note: Seawater desalination plant at Douira south of Agadir, whose water also irrigates the Chtouka vegetable farms.
